asset-finance|buying-equipment.title: Asset Finance for Buying Equipment | Loanleaf
asset-finance|buying-equipment.desc: How hire purchase and leasing work when a UK limited company buys machinery, tools or technology. One short form matches you with a specialist finance broker.
asset-finance|buying-equipment.lead: Spread the cost of a machine, tool or system over the years it earns for you, with the equipment itself acting as security.
intro: Equipment is the classic case for asset finance, because the lender can value the item, hold it as security and recover it if payments stop. That changes what the lender cares about. For a business buying a £60,000 CNC machine from an established supplier, the questions are mostly about the machine: what it is, how long it lasts, how easily it could be resold and what the supplier is charging. The company’s accounts still matter, but they sit alongside the asset rather than carrying the whole decision.

The usual aim is to match the agreement to the working life of the kit. Computers and software-heavy systems tend to be financed over a shorter term, while robust plant such as ovens, presses and lifts can often be spread over longer. A supplier quote or invoice, a deposit or first payment and a few months of accounts are normally where the process starts. A broker can then compare lenders who are comfortable with that particular type of equipment.
uses: A replacement that can’t wait
A bakery’s deck oven fails in the middle of the week. Financing the replacement from a supplier quote gets it installed without draining the cash that pays wages and flour.
A machine that adds capacity
A workshop with a full order book buys a second press brake. The extra output can start covering the payments while the original machine keeps running.
Used or auction kit
Many lenders will finance second-hand machinery, provided its age, condition and resale value are clear. Expect closer questions about where it came from and what it is worth.
Several items in one agreement
A new clinic or workshop may need a dozen pieces of kit from different suppliers. A broker can sometimes arrange them as a single facility rather than a separate agreement for each.
fit: Match the term to the useful life

Lenders generally prefer a term that ends well before the equipment is worn out or obsolete. For example, a £25,000 packaging line might be spread over five years, while a £25,000 IT refresh would more likely be agreed over three. A term longer than the asset’s life is hard to arrange.
What the lender checks about the kit

They look at the make, model, age and condition, the price against the market and the reputation of the supplier. Specialist or custom-built equipment is harder to value, which can mean a larger deposit or fewer lenders willing to take it on.
Deposit, VAT and the first payment

Agreements often start with a deposit or an advance rental, and with hire purchase VAT is usually paid at the start. Include both in your cash plan, because the first payment can be larger than the ones that follow.
considerations: Kit that is hard to resell

If the equipment is highly specialised or built into your premises, the lender cannot easily recover its money, so terms may be tighter. A broker might suggest a secured or unsecured business loan instead, which does not depend on the asset’s resale value.
Breakdowns and servicing stay with you

Payments continue whether the machine is running or not, and maintenance, insurance and repairs usually remain your responsibility. Ask the supplier about warranties and service contracts before you commit to a term.
Newer kit can overtake what you buy

In fast-moving areas such as imaging, printing or automation, a machine can feel dated before the agreement ends. A lease with an upgrade option may suit better than hire purchase, though you will not own the equipment at the end.
faqs: Can I finance equipment I have already bought?

Yes, in some cases. Asset refinance lets a company raise cash against equipment it has paid for and still uses. The lender usually asks for a valuation and may want to see proof of ownership. It is a different arrangement from financing the original purchase, so ask your broker how it would be structured.
Does the supplier need to be involved?

Usually, yes. For a new purchase the lender typically pays the supplier directly against an invoice, so the supplier needs to provide a clear quote and invoice. Private or auction sales can be financed by some lenders, but they ask for additional checks on ownership and condition.
Is leasing or hire purchase better for equipment?

It depends on how you use the kit. Hire purchase usually suits equipment you expect to keep for most of its life, because you own it at the end. Leasing can suit equipment that dates quickly or that you want to swap. Your accountant can advise on tax and VAT.
Can installation and training be included?

Sometimes. Lenders often finance the equipment itself and may include delivery or installation if they appear on the supplier’s invoice. Training, software licences and consumables are less likely to be covered, so you may need to find that cost separately.
How much equipment finance can a company get?

There is no single figure. It depends on the cost and type of equipment, any deposit, and the strength of your accounts. Smaller companies often finance single items, while established businesses can arrange facilities for a whole programme of purchases. A broker can tell you what is realistic for your figures.

asset-finance|buying-vehicles.title: Asset Finance for Buying Vehicles | Loanleaf
asset-finance|buying-vehicles.desc: How hire purchase, finance lease and contract hire work when a UK limited company buys vans, cars or lorries. Get matched with a specialist finance broker.
asset-finance|buying-vehicles.lead: Put vans, cars or lorries on the road and pay for them over the period they are in service, with the vehicle as security.
intro: Vehicles are one of the easiest things to finance, because they are widely traded, easy to value and carry a registration document. They also lose value quickly, and that shapes every agreement. A lender is thinking about what a three-year-old van will be worth when the agreement ends, how many miles it will have covered and whether your business is likely to look after it. The price, age and mileage of the vehicle often matter as much as your accounts.

There are three common routes. Hire purchase spreads the price and you own the vehicle at the end. A finance lease lets you use it for a set period, then sell, extend or hand it back. Contract hire is similar but often bundles servicing, with a mileage limit. Which one suits depends on how many miles you cover, how long you keep vehicles and whether you want to own them.
uses: A van for a trade business
An electrician or plumber with growing work needs a second van with racking. Financing it keeps cash available for tools, materials and the first weeks of wages.
Adding to a delivery fleet
A courier firm that wins a new route may need three more vans within weeks. Several vehicles can often be financed together, with the term set by how hard they will be worked.
Specialist bodies and conversions
Refrigerated vans, tail-lifts, tippers and recovery bodies cost more and resell less easily. Lenders may finance the conversion with the vehicle if it is on the same invoice.
Replacing an ageing fleet
A business with high repair bills on older lorries can settle the existing agreements and finance newer ones. A broker can check whether early settlement costs make this worthwhile.
fit: Term, mileage and depreciation

Commercial vehicles are commonly financed over a few years, with the length depending on type and use. For example, a £30,000 van used for local deliveries might run over four or five years, while a high-mileage vehicle may need a shorter term to stay ahead of its falling value.
What the lender looks at

They check the age and make of the vehicle, whether it is new or used, the dealer or seller and your company’s trading history. Many lenders cap the age of a used vehicle at the end of the agreement, so a six-year-old van may need a shorter term.
Balloon payments and deposits

A smaller monthly payment is possible if part of the price is left as a final balloon payment, but you must then pay it, refinance it or sell the vehicle. A deposit reduces the amount borrowed and may widen the choice of lenders.
considerations: Mileage and condition charges

Contract hire and some leases set a mileage limit and charge for excess miles and for damage beyond fair wear and tear. If your use is hard to predict, hire purchase avoids those charges, though payments are usually higher.
Owing more than the vehicle is worth
In the early years, a vehicle can be worth less than the amount still owed. That matters if you want to sell or swap it before the end, or if it is written off, so check what insurance would cover.
Running costs sit on top

Insurance, tax, servicing, tyres and fuel come in addition to the finance payment. For occasional use, hiring or renting may cost less than a long agreement, and an older vehicle may be better paid for from cash.
faqs: Should I choose hire purchase or contract hire?

Hire purchase suits a business that wants to own the vehicle and has no firm mileage limit. Contract hire can suit a business that replaces vehicles every few years and wants predictable running costs. The tax and VAT treatment differs, so it is worth asking your accountant before deciding.
Can I finance a used van or lorry?

Yes, many lenders will. They tend to set limits on age and mileage and may ask for a larger deposit. Buying from a reputable dealer usually makes the process simpler than a private sale, where lenders ask for more checks on ownership and condition.
Can I finance a conversion or tail-lift?

Often, if the work is invoiced alongside the vehicle or by an approved supplier. Lenders are more cautious about adaptations that cannot easily be resold. Mention any conversion at the start, because it can change which lenders are suitable. Tell your broker about the conversion at the start, so they can approach lenders who are comfortable with that kind of body.
What happens if I want to swap a vehicle early?

You would normally need to settle the agreement, and that can include charges for ending it early. If the vehicle is worth less than the settlement figure, you cover the difference. Ask for an early settlement figure before taking on a new agreement.
Does the company or a director own the vehicle?

With hire purchase, the company usually takes ownership once the final payment is made, and the finance company is the owner until then. Lenders sometimes ask a director to give a personal guarantee, especially for younger businesses or higher-value vehicles.

asset-finance|business-expansion.title: Asset Finance for Business Expansion | Loanleaf
asset-finance|business-expansion.desc: How asset finance covers the equipment and vehicles behind a second site, a bigger contract or new capacity, and what it can’t pay for. Free introduction.
asset-finance|business-expansion.lead: Finance the machines, vehicles and fit-out equipment behind your expansion, and keep cash for the costs that asset finance can’t cover.
intro: Expansion rarely has one price tag. A second site means rent, a deposit, stock, wages and marketing, but it also means a large amount of physical equipment: treatment couches, ovens, racking, a van, a till system. Asset finance covers that physical slice. It will not pay for the lease premium or the first month’s payroll, so it works best as one part of a plan rather than the whole answer.

Splitting the project this way can help. The equipment is financed against itself, which leaves cash and any other borrowing for the costs that have no asset behind them. Lenders will want to see how the new equipment earns money, so expect to explain the expected volumes or the contract it supports. Your existing record helps here: a business that has financed assets before and paid on time is usually easier to assess.
uses: Kitting out a second site
A physiotherapy clinic opening a second branch can finance treatment couches, diagnostic equipment and IT as a single package, and use its cash for the lease and the first months of running costs.
Capacity for a larger contract
A fabricator that wins a bigger order may need another machine and a forklift. Financing them lets the contract start without waiting for the first payment from the customer.
A vehicle for a new area
A cleaning or maintenance firm moving into a new region can finance vans for the extra crews, with the term matched to how long the vehicles will be in daily use.
Releasing cash from kit you own
Equipment that is fully paid for can be refinanced to raise a lump sum towards a deposit or fit-out, while you carry on using it. The payments then run alongside the new agreements.
fit: Cover the hard assets, not the whole project

For example, if a project costs £150,000 and £60,000 of it is equipment and vehicles, asset finance can address that £60,000. The remainder, such as the rent deposit, stock and early wages, needs to come from cash or another type of borrowing.
Phase payments with the build

Equipment often arrives in stages as a site is finished. Some lenders can start payments once an item is delivered and accepted, which keeps early cash from being tied up in agreements for kit still sitting in a warehouse.
Use what you already own

Lenders may take existing assets into account when assessing a larger request. A business with a good history of financed equipment can look stronger than one with none, so mention what you have financed before.
considerations: Payments start before the new revenue

Fixed payments begin whether or not the new site is trading to plan. Build a cautious forecast, and make sure the combined payments across all your agreements remain manageable if the ramp-up is slower than hoped.
Only recoverable assets qualify

Fixtures built into a leased building, marketing and refurbishment labour are hard to finance this way. If most of the budget sits in those items, a broker may suggest a term loan, a secured loan or a revolving credit facility alongside.
Buying more capacity than you can fill

Kit that stands idle still has to be paid for. Lenders can be wary of growth built on speculative demand, and you may be asked for evidence such as orders, contracts or the performance of your existing site.
faqs: Can asset finance pay for the whole expansion?

Rarely. It covers equipment and vehicles that a lender can hold as security. Rent, deposits, stock, wages and marketing normally need another source, such as cash reserves or a business loan. A broker can help you work out which parts of the budget suit which type of finance.
Will several agreements affect my borrowing?

Lenders will see your existing commitments and take them into account. Several agreements can still work if the business has strong cash flow, but the monthly total matters. Give your broker a full list of current payments at the start.
Can I finance equipment before the new site opens?

Often yes, though lenders look at the timing. Some are comfortable with deliveries ahead of opening, while others prefer to start once the equipment is in use. Ask about start dates and any initial rental or deferred first payment. Your broker can say which lenders are flexible about delivery dates.
What if I am expanding into a different sector?

The more unfamiliar the assets are to the lender, the more questions you can expect. Strong accounts and a clear plan help. If the new equipment is unusual, a specialist lender or a different structure may be a better fit than a mainstream provider.
Could I lease instead of buying for an expansion?

Leasing can keep payments lower and make it easier to scale up, hand back or upgrade kit as you learn what the new site needs. Hire purchase gives ownership at the end. Your accountant can say which is better for tax and cash flow.

asset-finance|refurbishing-premises.title: Asset Finance for Refurbishing Premises | Loanleaf
asset-finance|refurbishing-premises.desc: Which parts of a refit asset finance can cover, such as kitchens, plant and equipment, and which it can’t. Get matched with a specialist finance broker.
asset-finance|refurbishing-premises.lead: Asset finance can pay for the equipment inside a refit, but not the building work around it. Here is where the line usually falls.
intro: A refurbishment bill is a mix of very different things. Some of it is equipment a lender can identify, value and take back: a commercial kitchen, extraction, chairs and basins, lifting gear, lighting or heating plant. The rest is plastering, flooring, electrics, labour and design fees, which are bolted into a building and have no resale value on their own. Asset finance fits the first group well and the second hardly at all.

That makes the quote the most important document. A lender will want it broken down item by item, with the movable equipment separated from the building work. Because you are usually a tenant, they may also ask whether the landlord has any claim on items attached to the property. If equipment is financed separately, the other costs of the refit can be paid from cash, a loan or another form of finance.
uses: A new kitchen in a restaurant refit
Ovens, fryers, extraction and refrigeration are standard financeable assets. A £45,000 kitchen can be spread over several years, which leaves cash for the dining room and decoration.
Salon, clinic or gym equipment
Styling chairs, basins, couches or fitness machines are movable and valued easily. They can be financed separately from the shopfitting, with the term set by the equipment’s expected life.
Workshop plant and extraction
A garage or manufacturing unit upgrading lifts, compressors or dust extraction can often finance the plant itself, even if the unit is being reconfigured around it.
Heating, cooling and lighting systems

Some lenders will finance energy-efficient plant such as LED lighting, air handling or heat pumps when it is supplied and installed as equipment. They look closely at how the system is fixed and who owns it.
fit: Itemise the quote

Ask the contractor to separate equipment from construction. For example, if a £90,000 refit includes £35,000 of kitchen and bar equipment, asset finance can focus on that £35,000. A single lump-sum price makes it hard for a lender to see what they would be securing.
Landlord and fixtures

Items fixed to a rented building can become the landlord’s property or be difficult to remove. Lenders may ask for a landlord waiver or confirmation that the equipment can be taken back, so raise this early with your landlord.
Remaining lease length

A lender will not usually finance equipment for longer than you are likely to remain in the premises. If your lease has three years left, a seven-year agreement on fixed plant will be hard to arrange.
considerations: The biggest costs may not qualify

Labour, fabric repairs and fees are often the largest part of a refit and cannot normally be financed this way. If most of the project is building work, a secured or unsecured business loan may suit better, and a broker can compare the two.
Payments while the site is closed
A refit that closes the business for a few weeks means payments on the equipment may start before any takings do. Ask about a deferred first payment or a start date that follows reopening.
Equipment you may not be able to remove

If financed items are bolted in, the lender may find them hard to recover, and you could face questions about what happens if you leave the premises before the agreement ends. Check insurance and removal terms before signing.
faqs: Can asset finance pay for shopfitting?

Usually not. Shopfitting, flooring, partitions and decoration become part of the building and can’t easily be resold, so lenders rarely treat them as security. Free-standing equipment such as counters, display units, chairs and machines is more likely to qualify. A broker may suggest a loan for the building work.
Do I need my landlord’s permission?

Not always, but it helps. For equipment that is clearly movable, many lenders do not need it. For items fixed to the building, they may ask for a waiver or evidence that the equipment can be removed. Check your lease, and speak to the landlord early.
Can I finance second-hand equipment for a refit?

Yes, often. Lenders look at age, condition and resale value, and may want to see the seller’s invoice. Reconditioned kitchen and bar equipment is commonly financed, though the shorter remaining life of used items means a shorter term. Ask for the equipment to be listed separately on the invoice.
What if the refurbishment goes over budget?

The finance usually covers only the amount on the supplier’s invoice. Extra costs would come from cash or another source. It is sensible to keep a contingency and to discuss any variations with your broker before the invoice is issued.
Would a loan be simpler for a refit?

A business loan is one amount that can be spent on anything, including labour, so it avoids the line-drawing. It may cost more or ask for other security, and the repayments are not tied to the equipment’s life. A broker can compare both against your plans.

asset-finance|working-capital.title: Asset Finance for Working Capital | Loanleaf
asset-finance|working-capital.desc: How refinancing or sale and leaseback can raise cash from equipment you own, and when asset finance is the wrong tool for a cash flow gap. Free to use.
asset-finance|working-capital.lead: Raise cash against equipment you already own, or keep cash in the business by financing new kit, and know when that isn’t the right tool.
intro: Asset finance is not designed for day-to-day cash flow, but it can help in two ways. The first is asset refinance, where a lender advances cash against vehicles or equipment your company owns outright, often through a sale and leaseback. You keep using the kit, receive a lump sum and repay over an agreed term. The second is quieter: financing new purchases rather than paying cash for them, so that money stays available for wages and suppliers.

Both work because of something the business already has or is buying, which is a different basis from lending against your sales or your cash flow. The lender will value the equipment, perhaps independently, and the amount raised reflects that valuation, not the size of your gap. That makes it well suited to a one-off need and poorly suited to a problem that comes back every quarter. A broker can help judge which side of that line your situation falls on.
uses: Raising cash from a paid-off fleet
A haulier with several lorries that are fully paid for can refinance some of them to raise a lump sum. The lorries stay on the road while the payments are spread across the term.
Sale and leaseback of machinery
A manufacturer sells a press or production line to a lender and leases it straight back. The business gets cash and keeps production running, though it no longer owns the machine outright.
Keeping cash by financing new kit
Rather than paying £30,000 outright for a new vehicle, financing it leaves that amount in the bank for wages, supplier bills or a slow month.
Bridging a one-off squeeze
A company waiting on a large delayed payment may use refinanced equipment to cover the gap, provided there is a clear route to repay the agreement when the money arrives.
fit: Valuation sets the limit

The lender usually advances part of what the asset is worth, based on a valuation. Older or specialist kit raises less, and equipment already financed to someone else cannot be used again. The sum raised may differ from what you hoped for.
A fixed term, not a flexible one

Unlike an overdraft or invoice facility, asset refinance is a lump sum with a repayment schedule. That suits a defined need. If cash flow dips and recovers throughout the year, a revolving arrangement may match it better.
Companies with assets but tight cash

This tends to suit asset-heavy businesses such as hauliers, farms, contractors and manufacturers. Lenders still look at your trading record and ability to make the payments, so the equipment helps but does not replace that assessment.
considerations: Turning a gap into a fixed commitment

A temporary shortage becomes a payment that runs for years. If the underlying problem is slow-paying customers or low margins, the cash raised will run out and the payments remain. Look at the cause first, perhaps with your accountant.
Giving up ownership

In a sale and leaseback, the lender owns the equipment during the agreement. You may buy it back at the end, subject to the terms, or hand it over. Check what the end-of-term options cost, and how they affect your accounts.
Other lenders may see the commitment

Pledging existing equipment limits what you can offer others, and the new payments show up when you apply elsewhere. If you plan to borrow more soon, discuss the order of things with a broker before committing.
faqs: What is sale and leaseback?

The company sells an asset it owns to a lender and leases it straight back, so it keeps using the asset. The lender pays a lump sum and the company makes regular rental payments. It is a way to release the value tied up in equipment, with ownership held by the lender during the agreement.
How much cash can I raise against equipment?

It depends on the valuation of the equipment, its age and type, and on the strength of the business. The amount is usually a share of the asset’s value, not the full figure. A broker can tell you what is likely once they know what you own.
Do I need an independent valuation?

Often, particularly for higher-value machinery or a mixed fleet. Some lenders use guide prices for common vehicles instead. Who pays for the valuation varies, so ask for this to be explained at the start. Often, particularly for higher-value machinery or a mixed fleet, because the lender wants a reliable figure to lend against. Some lenders use guide prices for common vehicles instead. Who pays for the valuation varies between lenders, so ask for this to be explained at the start.
Is asset finance suitable for a recurring cash gap?

Usually not. A lump sum with fixed payments suits a single need. If you regularly wait for customers to pay, invoice finance or a revolving credit facility is more likely to follow the pattern of your cash flow. A broker can explain the difference.
Will refinancing equipment affect my other borrowing?

It can. The new agreement appears on your credit file and in your accounts, and the equipment may no longer be available as security for another lender. If you expect to need further borrowing, mention it up front. A broker can explain what a lender is likely to see.

invoice-finance|working-capital.title: Invoice Finance for Working Capital | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|working-capital.desc: How invoice factoring and discounting turn 30, 60 and 90-day customer terms into usable cash, and what limits the amount a facility can release.
invoice-finance|working-capital.lead: Release the cash sitting in unpaid invoices, and see which invoices, customers and terms decide how much that cash is.
intro: For many B2B companies, working capital is simply a matter of waiting. If a firm invoices £100,000 a month on 60-day terms, around £200,000 is always owed to it and not yet in the bank, however profitable the work. Invoice finance lets you borrow against that unpaid money, so the cash arrives soon after you invoice. As the ledger grows, the available cash grows with it, which is why the facility tends to move with the business.

The amount released depends on the quality of your customers, not just on your own accounts. A provider reviews who owes you, how reliably they pay and whether one customer makes up most of the ledger. Invoices that are disputed, very old or owed by customers it will not cover are excluded. So a facility on paper may be larger than the amount that proves usable in practice. Ask what share of your ledger would actually be eligible.
uses: Meeting payroll while customers take 60 days
A marketing agency pays wages monthly but is paid by clients after two months. Advancing against each invoice means pay day no longer depends on a client’s accounts team.
Replacing an overdraft at its limit
When an overdraft is full every month, a facility linked to the ledger can offer a limit that tracks sales instead of a fixed figure agreed in the past.
Coping with a seasonal peak in invoicing
A business that invoices heavily in the autumn can draw more when it needs it, and the amount falls back as customers pay, so you are not paying for borrowing in quieter months.
Financing one large slow-paying customer
With selective finance, you can advance against invoices to a single customer on 90-day terms, and leave the rest of the ledger alone.
fit: The ledger sets the ceiling

A provider usually advances a large share of each approved invoice, often 80 to 90%, so £150,000 of eligible invoices could release roughly £120,000 to £135,000. Invoices that are disputed, overdue or owed by excluded customers don’t count.
Whole ledger or selected invoices

A whole-ledger facility usually costs less per invoice and supports ongoing needs. Selective or spot finance gives control over what is financed and suits occasional gaps, though each invoice tends to cost more.
Concentration and customer quality

If one customer makes up most of your sales, the provider will usually set a limit for that customer, which restricts the facility. A spread of reliable customers is looked on more favourably than a single large one.
considerations: Cost grows as you use it

Fees are normally linked to turnover and the amount advanced, so the more you finance, the more you pay. Work out the cost at your expected volumes, and compare it with the margin on the work being financed.
Not every invoice is suitable
Consumer sales, staged payments, retentions and invoices payable only on completion can be hard to finance. If your income comes mostly from cards, a merchant cash advance may fit better.
Minimum terms and notice periods
Many facilities carry a minimum period and charges for leaving early. Read the notice terms and ask how fees work if your sales fall below the level the facility was set up for.
faqs: How long does it take to get cash after invoicing?

Once a facility is in place, the advance is often paid within a day or two of submitting an approved invoice. The set-up itself often takes a few weeks, because the provider reviews your ledger and customers first, so it helps to arrange it before the need is urgent.
Can I finance only some customers?

Yes. Some facilities cover your whole ledger, while selective invoice finance lets you choose invoices or customers. Selective is more flexible but usually costs more per invoice. Providers may also exclude customers they consider high-risk, so ask which of yours would be covered.
What happens if a customer doesn’t pay?

With most facilities you remain responsible, and the provider can reclaim the advance on an invoice that isn’t paid. Bad debt protection or credit insurance can cover this, at extra cost. Check how long the provider waits before reclaiming an advance.
Does invoice finance replace an overdraft?

It can do the same job, but it is secured on your invoices and can affect other lenders who have a charge over the same assets. Some businesses keep both. A broker can explain how existing borrowing would interact with a facility.
Is invoice finance suitable for a small business?

Many providers have minimum turnover or invoice volumes, and some have minimum fees, which can be hard to justify for very small sales ledgers. Selective finance has lower thresholds. A broker will know which providers work with a company of your size.

invoice-finance|hiring-staff.title: Invoice Finance for Hiring Staff | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|hiring-staff.desc: How invoice finance helps agencies, consultancies and contractors pay new hires before customers pay, and why it can’t cover the weeks before the first invoice.
invoice-finance|hiring-staff.lead: Pay new people on time while their work is still waiting to be paid for, if the hires produce the invoices.
intro: Invoice finance fits hiring best when the new people generate the invoices. A recruitment agency pays temporary workers every week and invoices clients monthly on 30-day terms. A consultancy hires engineers who bill by the day. In both, payroll goes out long before the matching invoice is paid, and each extra hire widens the gap. Advancing cash against those invoices lets the company keep paying staff on time while it waits.

It does less for hires who don’t bill directly, such as an office manager or a marketing lead, because the facility only grows when sales do. It also cannot pay for the weeks before a first invoice exists, since nothing has been raised to borrow against. A company planning several hires at once should look at the whole timeline of costs, and separate what an invoice facility can pay for from what it can’t.
uses: Weekly pay for agency temps
A staffing agency places twenty temporary workers who are paid every Friday, while the client is invoiced monthly. An advance on each invoice funds the payroll between billing and payment.
A consultancy adding billable staff
A firm that hires three engineers for a new contract can finance each monthly invoice as it is raised, rather than carrying their salaries for two months of customer terms.
Seasonal labour
A business that needs extra people for a busy quarter can fund them from the invoices that work generates, then let the facility shrink as the season ends.
Covering employer costs on top of pay
Employer National Insurance, pension contributions and holiday pay arrive alongside wages. When the invoices include those costs, the advance covers them too.
fit: The advance follows the invoice

For example, if a new hire is billed at £4,000 a month and the provider advances 85% of each approved invoice, about £3,400 is available soon after invoicing, rather than after the customer’s 45 days. The gap becomes shorter, though the remaining 15% still waits.
The lead-in period isn’t covered

A new hire might spend a month on onboarding or waiting for a start date before they bill. That period has no invoice to borrow against, so it needs cash or a different type of finance, such as an unsecured business loan.
What the provider checks

They look at the customers who will be paying, how long they take and whether the contract supports the work. A new contract with a customer the provider has already approved is easier to fit than a hire without a named client.
considerations: Margin has to absorb the fees

Each invoice carries a fee and a charge on the money advanced. If the margin on a placement or project is thin, those costs can take a large share of it. Check the numbers on a typical contract before you commit.
Hires that don’t bill

Support roles, managers and trainees add costs without adding invoices, so a facility won’t grow to match. If most of the hiring is non-billable, a business loan or revolving facility may serve better, and a broker can compare them.
Customers who dispute or delay

If a client queries hours or delays approval, the invoice may be excluded from the facility while you still pay the person who did the work. Keep timesheets and approvals tidy, and check how the provider treats disputed items.
faqs: Can invoice finance pay my staff before I invoice?

No. The advance is made against an invoice that has been raised, so there needs to be a delivered piece of work and a bill. For the period before that, you would need cash or a different kind of finance. A broker can help work out the size of that gap.
Is invoice finance common in recruitment?

Yes, it is widely used by agencies, because they pay workers weekly and invoice clients later. Providers who specialise in the sector understand timesheets, client approvals and PAYE obligations, and a broker can introduce you to those that do. Ask the broker which providers have experience of your type of hire.
Does it matter if my staff are on fixed salaries?

It can. Fixed salaries and monthly invoices make the gap predictable, which helps with planning. But if a salaried employee is not billable for some months, the invoices don’t rise to match the cost. Keep a margin for that in your forecast.
Could hiring ahead of a contract be financed this way?

Not directly. Until an invoice exists, there is nothing for the provider to advance against. Once the first invoices are approved and issued, the facility starts to help. Some businesses use a separate short-term loan to cover that opening period.
Will my clients know I use invoice finance?

With factoring they will, because the provider collects payment. With confidential invoice discounting, you continue to collect payments yourself. Some agencies prefer the confidential option, though it is usually offered to more established businesses with a longer record. Ask which option each provider offers.

invoice-finance|buying-stock.title: Invoice Finance for Buying Stock | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|buying-stock.desc: How invoice finance helps wholesalers, manufacturers and distributors restock faster by releasing cash after each sale, and what it can’t do before you sell.
invoice-finance|buying-stock.lead: Restock sooner by releasing the cash from invoices already raised, rather than waiting for customers to pay.
intro: Invoice finance does not pay for stock directly. What it does is shorten the cycle that stock runs through: you buy, make, deliver, invoice, then wait for payment before the next purchase. By advancing most of an invoice within days of raising it, the facility returns the cash soon after delivery, ready to buy the next batch. The shorter the wait, the more often the same money can be used.

This suits businesses that sell to other businesses on credit, such as a food distributor supplying restaurants or a manufacturer selling to retailers. It does not suit stock bought long before it sells, or sold to consumers at the till. Where a company must pay a supplier before it has an order or a customer to invoice, a broker might suggest other options such as purchase order finance, trade finance or a term loan.
uses: Restocking on 60-day customer terms
A wholesaler delivers £40,000 of goods to a retailer who pays in two months. Advancing against the invoice funds the next order from the supplier rather than leaving it to wait.
Keeping production running
A manufacturer buying raw materials weekly can use each invoice’s advance to buy the next round, so a large customer’s payment terms don’t slow the line.
Taking a large order from a new customer
Once a customer is approved, a large order can be financed as it is delivered. The business buys the materials for the next order while the first invoice is still waiting to be paid.
Paying suppliers early
Prompt payment can win a settlement discount or better prices from suppliers. Funds released by a facility can make that routine, and the saving can offset part of the cost.
fit: It follows the sale, not the purchase

If you must pay for goods up front and sell them months later, there is no invoice to borrow against during that period. The facility works best when stock turns into an invoice quickly, typically within weeks.
A cycle that repeats

For example, a distributor that turns stock into invoices every three weeks can recycle the same advanced cash around the cycle several times a quarter. This is where a facility earns its cost, compared with a one-off loan.
Customers decide the limit

The provider approves each customer and sets a limit on the debt it will fund. A new retailer without a payment record may start with a modest limit, which restricts how much stock cycle the facility can support at first.
considerations: Stock isn’t the security

The facility is built on invoices, not the stock itself. Some providers can add stock finance as a further layer, though this is a separate arrangement with its own terms. Ask if it is available for your type of goods.
Slow-moving or seasonal stock

Goods that sit for months before sale are not helped, and a seasonal business may have a long wait before the first invoice. A broker may suggest a short-term loan or trade finance to cover that stretch.
Costs should fit your margin

Fees are charged on invoices and on the advance, so a business with a thin margin on each order feels them more. Compare the cost with the margin earned on the stock, and with a loan taken for the same purpose.
faqs: Can invoice finance pay my supplier directly?

Not in the usual form. It advances cash against invoices you have already raised, which you then use to pay suppliers. Trade finance and purchase order finance are different products that can pay suppliers earlier, and a broker may raise them if you buy against confirmed orders.
Is invoice finance suitable for an online shop?

Generally not, because sales are paid at checkout rather than on credit terms, so there are no invoices to finance. A business that sells to consumers may find a merchant cash advance or a business loan fits better. Online businesses that sell to trade customers on terms are the exception.
Does it help with bulk-buying discounts?

Indirectly. If a facility has released cash from earlier sales, you may have the money to take a bulk discount without waiting. The saving should be compared with the fees you pay. If the discount is small, the cost of the facility could outweigh it.
What about stock that is imported?

Imports often need payment well before the goods arrive and sell, so there can be a long gap with no invoice. A broker may suggest trade finance for that period and invoice finance once the stock is sold. Lead times and currency can affect which providers will help.
Can invoice finance cover VAT on invoices?

Invoice values normally include VAT, and the advance is calculated on the approved invoice. The provider’s terms set out how VAT is treated, so check this with the provider and your accountant, particularly if you account for VAT in an unusual way.

invoice-finance|business-expansion.title: Invoice Finance for Business Expansion | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|business-expansion.desc: How an invoice finance facility grows with your sales when you win bigger customers or enter new markets, and why it won’t pay for sites or machinery.
invoice-finance|business-expansion.lead: Grow sales without growing the cash gap, because the facility rises as your invoices do.
intro: The risk with fast growth is not a lack of customers but a lack of cash while they pay. A company that doubles its sales also doubles the amount owed to it, and larger customers often pay more slowly. Invoice finance is built for this, because the amount available follows the sales ledger. There is no need to apply for a bigger loan each time the business gets bigger, since the facility expands as invoices are raised.

Its limits are just as clear. It funds the working capital that expansion creates, not the assets behind it. A second site, a new machine or an acquisition needs a different kind of finance. Providers also add each new customer to the facility one by one, so growth built on one new large customer can run into a credit limit. It is worth putting this in place before the big order arrives.
uses: Winning a bigger customer
A packaging manufacturer lands a national retailer that pays after 60 days. The facility advances cash as deliveries are invoiced, so the production costs for the following orders are met.
Selling to new markets
A company starting to export can finance invoices to overseas customers, though providers vary in the countries and currencies they cover and may apply different limits.
Moving from one-off jobs to contracts
A services firm that wins a year-long contract can invoice monthly and draw funds against each bill, rather than carrying the delivery costs for months.
Growth through several customers
A business adding many mid-sized customers builds a spread that providers look upon well, and the facility can extend as each is approved.
fit: Set it up before you need it

A facility often takes a few weeks to arrange, as the provider reviews your ledger and customers. Applying once a large order has been won, but before delivery, avoids a gap between the work and the cash.
Credit limits per customer

Each customer carries its own limit. For example, a provider might fund up to £100,000 of invoices to a single new customer, even if your total facility is higher. A large order from one buyer can then exceed what is available.
Scaling with the business

Whole-ledger facilities can expand as turnover grows, and many are reviewed periodically. Ask whether there is a minimum fee that would apply if sales fall below the level you set up for, since expansion plans can change.
considerations: It doesn’t pay for assets or premises

Invoice finance cannot fund a lease deposit, a refit or equipment. Most expansion projects need a mix of finance, and a broker can look at how an invoice facility sits alongside an asset finance agreement or a business loan.
Dependence on a few large buyers

Concentration limits mean a business with one dominant customer may find the facility smaller than expected. If a buyer is slow or disputes invoices, the facility is hit directly. Ask how the provider would treat a delay.
Longer terms and bigger fees

Larger customers often demand longer payment terms, which means each pound is financed for longer and costs more. Include the extended terms in your forecasts, rather than using the terms you have today.
faqs: Can I finance invoices to customers abroad?

Some providers do, for a range of countries, but conditions differ. They may require credit insurance, set lower limits or exclude some markets. If exporting is part of your plan, tell your broker which countries and currencies are involved at the start.
Will the facility grow automatically?

Usually the amount available rises as you raise more approved invoices, up to the limits set for the facility and for each customer. The overall limit may be reviewed, and a minimum fee may apply. Ask how both work in your case.
Is invoice finance good for a company with big contracts?

It can be, as it releases cash against each stage of invoicing. Contracts with staged payments, retentions or acceptance clauses are harder to finance, because the invoice may not be due until conditions are met. A broker can say how providers treat your type of contract.
Can it fund an acquisition?

Not usually. Invoice finance releases cash from an existing sales ledger and is not designed to buy a business. An acquisition tends to need a term loan or a secured arrangement, though the target’s own ledger might later be added to a facility.
What if my sales fall after expansion?

Fees are tied to turnover and the amount used, so they reduce as you use less, though minimum fees and notice periods can apply. A shortfall may also reduce the amount available. Read the terms for minimum charges before agreeing to a long commitment.

invoice-finance|paying-a-tax-bill.h1: Invoice finance for paying a tax bill
invoice-finance|paying-a-tax-bill.title: Invoice Finance for Paying a Tax Bill | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|paying-a-tax-bill.desc: Why a VAT bill often comes from invoices customers haven’t paid, how invoice finance can release that cash, and why timing matters. Free introduction.
invoice-finance|paying-a-tax-bill.lead: A VAT bill often comes from invoices that haven’t been paid yet, which is exactly the cash invoice finance can release.
intro: For many B2B companies, the tax bill and the cash gap are the same problem. Under standard VAT accounting, a business owes HMRC the VAT on an invoice for the quarter in which it was raised, whether or not the customer has paid. A strong quarter of sales on 60-day terms can therefore produce a large bill while much of the money is still with customers. Advancing cash against those invoices closes the gap directly.

Timing is the catch. A new facility often takes a few weeks to arrange, so it will not rescue a payment due in days. It also doesn’t line up with every tax: corporation tax depends on profit rather than unpaid invoices. A company that sees the bill coming can set up a facility in time, while a company already close to the deadline may need a different route, such as speaking to HMRC about a payment plan.
uses: A quarterly VAT payment
A business invoices £200,000 plus VAT in a quarter, but customers have paid only a third. Drawing against the unpaid invoices releases cash to pay the VAT on all of them.
PAYE and National Insurance after a busy month
Higher payroll from extra hours or hires means a bigger PAYE bill. If that work is invoiced but unpaid, an advance can cover the HMRC payment.
Avoiding a late payment
Paying HMRC late can bring interest and penalties. Using an existing facility to meet the due date can be cheaper than falling behind, once you compare the charges.
Smoothing a repeated pattern
A business that faces the same large VAT bill every quarter may keep a facility in place to even it out, instead of arranging cash each time.
fit: Match the facility to the quarter

For example, if £90,000 of VAT falls due in six weeks, and the provider advances 85% of £400,000 of approved invoices, the cash is there to meet it. But an application needs to start well ahead of the date.
Existing facilities are easier to use

A business that already has a facility can often draw on newly raised invoices soon after they are approved. If you are considering one for this reason, look at it as a permanent source of working capital, not a one-time fix.
Which tax is it?

VAT and PAYE bills can often be linked to invoicing. Corporation tax is based on profit and arrives after the year-end, so the link to unpaid invoices is weaker. A broker may suggest a short-term loan or an instalment arrangement instead.
considerations: It may arrive too late

If the deadline is days away, set-up times can rule invoice finance out. Contact HMRC early, as it may offer a payment arrangement. A broker can say whether another form of finance could be arranged in time.
Don’t treat it as the cure

If tax bills keep exceeding what you have set aside, the cause is cash planning or margins, not the invoices. Borrowing to pay the same bill each quarter adds cost. An accountant can help set money aside from each sale.
Fees and long commitments

A facility set up for one bill may carry a minimum term and charges. Weigh these against the cost of a payment plan with HMRC, or a short-term loan, particularly if you don’t expect to use the facility again.
faqs: Can I use invoice finance to pay HMRC?

Yes, the cash you receive is yours to use, and some businesses use it to pay VAT or PAYE. The provider’s concern is the invoice, not what the money is spent on. Check the facility terms, and keep up with other commitments so that borrowing doesn’t fall behind.
Why does a VAT bill arise before customers pay?

Under standard VAT accounting, VAT is due for the period in which the invoice is issued, not when the customer pays. Some small businesses can use cash accounting, which ties the bill to payment. Your accountant can say which scheme applies to you.
How long does it take to arrange invoice finance?

Set-up often takes a few weeks, because the provider reviews your ledger, your customers and your accounts. Once the facility is live, advances are often paid within a day or two of an invoice being approved. That is why starting early matters.
Is a payment plan with HMRC cheaper?

It may be, but it depends on the circumstances and the interest HMRC charges. It also needs HMRC’s agreement. Invoice finance releases money you are already owed, whereas a payment plan delays the bill. A broker or accountant can help you weigh the two.
Does HMRC care how I pay the bill?

HMRC needs the payment in full and on time, and doesn’t mind where the money comes from. If you are using a facility, make sure the advance is available before the due date, because a payment that arrives late still counts as late.

merchant-cash-advance|working-capital.h1: Merchant cash advance for working capital
merchant-cash-advance|working-capital.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Working Capital | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|working-capital.desc: How a merchant cash advance covers rent, suppliers and quiet months for businesses with steady card takings, and what the fixed cost means for your margin.
merchant-cash-advance|working-capital.lead: Cover quiet months and bills out of future card takings, with repayments that rise and fall with the till.
intro: A café, salon or shop with steady card sales can still hit a run of weeks where rent, suppliers and wages outrun takings. A merchant cash advance provides a lump sum against the card sales you expect, and repays itself as a share of each transaction. There is no fixed monthly instalment to find in a slow week, because a quieter week simply repays less. That is the main difference from a conventional loan.

The total repayable is agreed at the start as a fixed fee on top of the advance, so a slower period lengthens the repayment rather than raising the cost. Providers look at recent card terminal statements to decide how much to offer. If most of your income arrives by bank transfer or on invoice, the history they rely on isn’t there, and a different product such as invoice finance is more likely to fit.
uses: Getting through a quiet season
A seaside café that trades weakly from November to February can use an advance to meet rent and supplier bills, and repay from the busier weeks that follow.
Covering a supplier price rise
When costs go up faster than prices, a restaurant may need cash to carry the gap while menus are reworked. The advance buys time without a fixed monthly charge.
A delayed payment elsewhere
A business that also sells on credit, and is waiting on a late invoice, can bridge the shortfall from its card income instead of missing a bill.
Replacing an expensive stop-gap
Instead of overdrafts or late fees, an advance can give a single sum and a known total to repay. The cost still needs comparing, as it is not always lower.
fit: The share is taken from every sale

For example, if 12% of each card payment goes towards repayment, then £1,000 of takings leaves £880 for the business that day. Check that the margin on your sales can bear that reduction without leaving costs uncovered.
Size follows your takings

The amount offered is linked to your recent average monthly card sales, so a business with consistent trade is offered more than one with erratic months. A few strong recent months can help a quiet spell’s application.
Fixed total, variable time
An advance repays more slowly in a poor month and faster in a busy one, but the total repayable agreed at the start stays the same. Ask whether there is a minimum amount due each month.
considerations: Quick repayment doesn’t cut the cost

Because the fee is fixed, repaying early does not usually reduce it. A business that recovers quickly can end up paying a high effective cost. Ask for the total repayable and compare it with a loan or revolving facility.
Less cash from every sale

The share taken is gone from every day’s takings until the advance clears. If your cash is already tight, this can feel heavier than a monthly payment. A broker may suggest a revolving credit facility for a recurring need.
Switching terminals
Many providers collect through your card terminal, or require you to stay with a certain provider. Moving terminals mid-agreement can breach it, so check the terms before you commit to a change.
faqs: Is this a good fit if I mostly take bank transfers?

Usually not. Providers look at card transactions, so a business paid by bank transfer or invoice has little for them to assess. Invoice finance or an unsecured business loan is more likely to suit. A broker can say which route works for your mix of payments.
What happens in a month with very low takings?

The share taken falls with takings, so you repay less, and the advance takes longer to clear. The total repayable normally stays the same. Some agreements have minimum payments or an expected end date, so check them before you sign.
How is the cost shown?

Usually as a total repayable figure, such as the advance plus a fixed fee, rather than an interest rate. That makes direct comparison difficult. Ask the broker to show it as a total in pounds and the expected repayment period, and compare against other options.
Can I take another advance while repaying one?

Some providers allow a top-up after part of the advance is repaid, while others don’t. Several advances at once can take a large share of your takings, and lenders will see them. Ask the broker how any further borrowing would be treated.
Is a personal guarantee required?

Sometimes. Merchant cash advances can be unsecured against property, but some providers ask a director to guarantee them. Read the agreement for any guarantee and for what happens if the business stops trading with the advance outstanding. Ask your broker to point out any guarantee before you sign.

merchant-cash-advance|buying-stock.h1: Merchant cash advance for buying stock
merchant-cash-advance|buying-stock.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Buying Stock | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|buying-stock.desc: How retailers, bars and restaurants can pay for stock with a merchant cash advance repaid from card sales, and when stock turns too slowly for it to work.
merchant-cash-advance|buying-stock.lead: Buy stock ahead of a busy spell and repay from the card sales that stock generates, as it sells.
intro: Stock and card takings move together in a way that suits this kind of finance. A gift shop buying for Christmas, a bar stocking up before the summer or a bike shop ordering for spring is paying for goods that will mostly be sold over the till within weeks. An advance repaid as a share of card sales follows that sell-through: busy days repay more, slow days less. Used well, it ties repayment to the sale of the goods it paid for.

The test is how fast the stock turns. A fixed fee on a short holding period can be worth paying, while the same fee on goods that sit for six months is hard to justify. The structure also doesn’t suit businesses that sell mainly to other businesses on credit, because their income does not pass through a card terminal. For them, a broker may point towards invoice finance or a business loan instead.
uses: Christmas stock for a shop
A homewares retailer places its autumn order in September and sells most of it in November and December. An advance covers the order, and card sales over those weeks repay it.
Restocking a bar before summer
A pub in a tourist town orders extra drinks and food supplies ahead of the season. Repayments follow the busy trading weeks.
Taking a supplier’s bulk deal
A one-off discount for buying a large quantity may beat the fee, if the stock sells fairly soon. It should be calculated before you go ahead.
Launching a new range
A boutique adding a clothing line can fund the first order and repay from its sales. If the range sells slowly, the repayments stretch out with it.
fit: Does the saving beat the fee?

For example, a retailer borrowing £15,000 for stock that sells in two months should compare the total repayable with the extra margin earned from having the stock. If the fee costs more than the gain, a cheaper form of finance may be better.
Stock that sells through quickly

Fast-selling lines suit this structure, as the advance is repaid within weeks. Slow lines stretch repayment, and the share of sales taken continues while the shelf stays full. Check how many weeks of sales it would take to clear a slow line.
Sized on existing takings
The offer is based on your recent card sales rather than the stock you plan to buy. A larger order than your takings can support may not be fully funded, which a broker can help you estimate.
considerations: Ordering more than you can sell
A readily available advance can make it tempting to overbuy. Unsold stock still has to be paid for, with a share of every sale going to repayment. Base the order on past sales, not on hopes.
Perishable or fashion-led goods
Food that expires or clothing that dates loses its value fast. If the stock doesn’t sell, the money is spent but the goods have not earned it back, so be cautious with short-lived lines.
Supplier credit may cost less

Asking suppliers for longer payment terms can be cheaper than any form of borrowing. A broker may also suggest a revolving credit facility if you restock regularly and want to draw and repay as needed.
faqs: How is a merchant cash advance different from a stock loan?

A stock loan is usually repaid by fixed instalments, and the stock may be part of the security. A merchant cash advance is repaid from a share of card takings, with no fixed instalment. Its cost is a fixed fee, so it needs comparing as a total rather than a rate.
Can I use it for a bulk purchase from overseas?

You can use the cash as you wish, but overseas orders often need payment well before the stock arrives and sells, and the share of sales is still being taken meanwhile. Check the cash flow across the whole delay before using an advance this way.
Is it suitable for an online-only shop?

Often, if payments pass through a card terminal or payment processor that the provider works with. Some providers offer revenue-based finance for online sellers. A broker can say who works with your payment set-up. Often, as long as payments pass through a card terminal or payment processor that the provider works with. Some providers offer revenue-based finance for online sellers instead. A broker can say who works with your payment set-up.
What if sales are lower than I expected?

You repay less each day, so the advance takes longer to clear, and the total stays the same. The danger is a run of poor weeks with unsold stock and a continuing share of sales going out. Keep a margin in your plan for that.
Could I repay early to save money?

Usually the fee is fixed, so repaying early does not reduce it, and an early finish can leave a high effective cost. Some providers offer a discount for early settlement, so ask whether this is possible before you agree. Ask about it up front.

merchant-cash-advance|refurbishing-premi.h1: Merchant cash advance for refurbishing premises
merchant-cash-advance|refurbishing-premi.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Refurbishing Premises | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|refurbishing-premi.desc: How a merchant cash advance can pay for a refit when a venue stays open or closes briefly, and how disruption to card takings affects repayment.
merchant-cash-advance|refurbishing-premi.lead: Pay for a refit from future card takings, and plan the work so the repayments don’t land while the doors are shut.
intro: A refit is unusual among business costs because it can interrupt the very income that repays it. A merchant cash advance takes a share of card sales, so if the venue is closed for two weeks there are no takings to repay from. That can feel like a pause, but the total is fixed and the lender will still expect repayment once you reopen. The advance itself isn’t secured on the building, so there is no need to involve the landlord.

This makes the timing of the work as important as the cost. A restaurant that refits in phases and trades throughout has a steady flow of card sales, while a salon that closes for a month has none. Providers assess recent trading rather than the project, so the amount offered reflects the business as it has been, not as the new fit-out may make it. It is worth applying while takings are still at their normal level.
uses: A phased refit of a restaurant
A restaurant refreshing its dining room can do it zone by zone, and trade through. Card sales continue, and repayments continue with them.
A short closure in a quiet month
A salon redecorating over a fortnight in January can take an advance beforehand and repay from the sales that follow reopening.
Updating a shop front and display
A retailer refreshing its frontage and lighting can fund the work while remaining open, with each day’s takings contributing to repayment.
Replacing flooring, seating and lighting
Items that are fixed to the premises are hard to finance as assets, but a cash advance can cover them, because it relies on your takings, not on the item.
fit: Takings during the works

For example, if a café normally takes £25,000 a month and closes for two weeks, repayments pause during the closure, then resume afterwards. The total stays fixed, so the delay means the advance runs for longer in calendar terms.
Open-ended costs

An advance is a fixed sum, so it should be sized with a margin for overruns. Refits commonly cost more than planned, and a second advance after the first may be harder to arrange while the first is still being repaid.
No security on the premises
Because it is based on card takings, it doesn’t depend on lease length or a landlord’s consent. That is useful for tenants, though your lease may still require permission for the works themselves.
considerations: The return isn’t guaranteed
A new look may lift sales, but not necessarily by enough to repay a fixed fee. Base the plan on takings as they are today, and treat any uplift as a bonus.
Closure and cash flow

If the venue closes, rent, wages and utilities carry on without takings. The advance has to cover the refit and the weeks of lost income. A broker may suggest a secured or unsecured loan if the closure is long.
Matching the term to the benefit

A refit lasts years, but an advance is usually repaid over months. This can make the repayments heavy compared with a loan spread over a longer term. Compare the total cost and the share of sales taken each day.
faqs: What if the refit keeps me closed longer than planned?

Repayments are taken from takings, so a longer closure means no repayment, but the total owed is unchanged and your costs continue. Providers may also have rules on the agreement’s timeline. Plan a buffer in your cash for overruns. Check what the agreement says.
Do I need my landlord’s consent for the advance?

Not for the advance, because it is not secured on the property. You may still need consent for the works themselves, under your lease, so check that first. Lenders of other types may ask about lease length. Your own broker or solicitor can confirm this.
Can I take an advance for a refit that hasn’t started?

Yes. The provider looks at your existing card sales, not at the project, so it can be arranged before work begins. Some people prefer to take it once quotes are agreed, so the amount matches the cost. Ask the broker how timing affects the amount.
Is asset finance cheaper for part of the refit?

It can be for equipment, as the asset acts as security, and terms are often longer. It will not cover labour or fixed items. Some businesses split the budget between asset finance for kit and an advance or loan for the rest.
Will a refit affect my card turnover assessment?

The provider will use recent history, so a temporary dip because of the works may count against you if you apply during or after it. If possible, apply while takings are at their normal level, before the closure. Some providers also look at the weeks just before applying.

merchant-cash-advance|buying-equipment.h1: Merchant cash advance for buying equipment
merchant-cash-advance|buying-equipment.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Buying Equipment | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|buying-equipment.desc: When a merchant cash advance suits an urgent equipment purchase, such as a broken oven or till system, and when asset finance would cost less over time.
merchant-cash-advance|buying-equipment.lead: Replace a broken oven, coffee machine or till system, and see how it compares with asset finance on cost.
intro: When a commercial oven, coffee machine or fridge fails, the question is how fast the business can trade again. An advance against card takings does not depend on the equipment, so it can be used for any supplier, including used kit, private sales and items a lender wouldn’t treat as security. The provider looks at your recent card sales, and the amount is not tied to a supplier invoice. The equipment itself does not need to be on any list.

That flexibility has a cost. Equipment finance can usually be spread over the life of the machine, with the item acting as security, which often makes it cheaper. An advance is typically repaid over months and carries a fixed fee, so the effective cost can be higher. It tends to make sense where asset finance isn’t available, where the equipment can’t be financed easily or where timing outweighs price. A broker can lay the two side by side.
uses: A breakdown in service
A café’s espresso machine fails before the weekend. An advance lets the owner buy a replacement from any supplier, and the new machine contributes to repayment through coffee sales.
Used or reconditioned equipment
Some lenders are cautious about older or reconditioned equipment, while an advance is based on takings, so a second-hand purchase doesn’t complicate it.
Equipment from several suppliers
Setting up a new kitchen from different sellers is simpler with one sum of cash than with a separate agreement for each item.
New till and payment systems
Replacing a till or card system can improve trading, and the benefit appears in the same card takings that repay the advance. Check that any new terminal fits the provider’s requirements.
fit: Short repayment, long-lived kit

A machine that lasts seven years is paid for in perhaps a year, so the repayments are heavy relative to its life. For example, £12,000 for an oven could be spread over several years with asset finance, but repaid in months here.
Time against cost

An advance may involve fewer documents than other finance, which can matter when a business can’t trade without the item. A broker can show what a comparison would cost in total pounds, so you can weigh time against price.
Based on trading, not on the item
The amount is linked to your average card takings. A purchase large in relation to your sales may exceed what a provider will offer, whereas asset finance considers the equipment’s value as well.
considerations: You own it, but the cost is higher

There is no residual value or lender ownership to worry about, since the machine is yours from the start. In return, you pay a fixed fee that can exceed the cost of financing the same kit over a longer term.
Reduced cash during repayment
A share of every sale goes towards repayment, which reduces day-to-day cash. If the new equipment won’t raise takings, that reduction is a pure cost. Check that the margin on sales can cope.
Not for equipment that doesn’t sell through the till

If the equipment supports back-office work, such as workshop tools used for repair jobs invoiced to other businesses, the card-based structure may not match. Asset finance or a loan is likely to be a better fit.
faqs: Is a merchant cash advance cheaper than asset finance?

Often not. Asset finance is secured on the equipment and can be spread over its working life, which tends to reduce the cost. An advance is quicker to arrange in some cases and doesn’t depend on the asset. Compare the total repayable in pounds for each option.
Can I use it to buy from a private seller?

Yes. The provider assesses your takings, not the purchase, so there is no supplier invoice requirement. Asset finance lenders are more cautious about private sales, which is one reason an advance appeals when you find a bargain. Keep a receipt or bill of sale for your records.
Does the equipment act as security?

Not normally. An advance relies on your future card sales and may carry a director’s guarantee, but it isn’t secured on the machine. That means the provider cannot take the item back, though other consequences apply if the agreement is breached.
What if the new equipment doesn’t raise sales?

The advance is still repaid from takings, and the total stays fixed. The share of sales taken reduces your cash whether or not the purchase has helped. A like-for-like replacement keeps trading going, but may not increase takings. Ask your broker to explain the options.
Can I finance installation and delivery?

Because the cash is yours to spend, yes, you can use it for delivery, installation or related costs. Asset finance lenders may only cover items on the supplier’s invoice. Keep the receipts in case the provider asks how the advance was used.

merchant-cash-advance|business-expansion.h1: Merchant cash advance for business expansion
merchant-cash-advance|business-expansion.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Business Expansion | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|business-expansion.desc: How a merchant cash advance sized on your existing card takings can help fund a second site or longer hours, and why a new site won’t count at first.
merchant-cash-advance|business-expansion.lead: Use the card takings of the business you have to help fund the next one, and know where the limits are.
intro: An advance is sized on what a business already takes, not on what the new site might. A restaurant opening a second branch is judged on the card sales of the first, and a new site has no history to show. So the offer reflects the established business, and the repayments are taken from every card payment, including those at the first site. In effect, the original site carries the cost of the second while it finds its feet.

That is the central fact for anyone using it to expand. It can suit a move that doesn’t need a large single sum, such as a pop-up, extended hours, a delivery operation or a small second unit. For a bigger project, the advance may be too small, and its short repayment period can strain the business. A broker may suggest combining it with asset finance for equipment or a term loan with a longer repayment period.
uses: A second small unit
A coffee shop opening a kiosk can fund the fit-out and first stock from an advance against the main café’s takings, with both sites’ sales going towards repayment once the kiosk is open.
Extending hours or adding a service
A bar adding food, or a salon offering evening sessions, can fund the equipment and early staffing costs and see whether the extra trade pays for itself.
Testing a new location
A pop-up or short lease lets a business trial a new area. An advance suits a shorter, smaller commitment better than a long-term loan.
Starting delivery or click-and-collect
A restaurant adding delivery can fund packaging, a scooter or a delivery tool, and repay from combined takings. Payments made through a delivery platform may not pass through the card terminal.
fit: The first site supports the second

For example, if the main café takes £35,000 a month and the advance takes 12% of each sale, around £4,200 a month goes to repayment. If the new site is slow, the existing site’s margin has to carry that, so test it.
Sized on history
Providers look at several months of card statements, so a business with a few strong recent months can be offered more. A recent dip, or a new terminal provider, may reduce what’s available.
A short repayment period

An advance is generally repaid over months, while an expansion can take a year or more to pay back. A broker may suggest a longer-term product for the main costs and an advance for a smaller, quick need.
considerations: Draining the site that works
A share of every sale from the profitable site funds the new one. If both struggle at once, there is little room. Build a cautious forecast, and leave enough cash for running costs.
Terminal and platform conditions

Many providers need you to take card payments through a specific provider, and a second site may use a different set-up. Check that the new location’s payments will be covered in the way the agreement expects.
Stacking advances

Taking a second advance on top of the first adds to the share of takings going out. Lenders will see the commitments. For a larger project, a loan with a defined term and fixed repayments may give more predictable cash flow.
faqs: Will takings at the new site count towards my offer?

Not at first. Providers rely on past card statements, so a new site has no history. After a few months of trading, its takings can be included if you apply again, which may let you raise a larger amount. A broker can tell you how soon that might be.
Can I open the new site under a different terminal provider?

You may, but check the agreement first. Some advances are collected through a specific terminal provider, and changing could breach the terms. Ask the broker how a second site, with a separate set-up, would be handled. Ask for a clear explanation of how many sites the advance covers.
Is a merchant cash advance enough for a full second restaurant?

Often not. A second restaurant usually needs a substantial sum for the lease, fit-out, equipment and wages. An advance sized on one site’s takings may cover only part of that, so it commonly sits alongside other finance, such as asset finance for kit.
How does an advance compare with a term loan for growth?

A term loan has fixed instalments over a defined period, often longer than an advance, and the cost is an interest rate. An advance moves with your sales but is repaid over a shorter time. A broker can compare the total cost and the effect on cash flow.
Does the business need to be profitable to qualify?

Providers focus on card takings rather than profit, so a business can qualify without strong profits. But repayments still come from your cash, and an unprofitable business may struggle with a share of every sale going out. Look at your margins first.
